# RSI as Measure, Not Dimension

**Decision.** Store the 14-day relative strength index as a nullable numeric **column on the fact
table** `dw.FACT_QUOTES`, and push the overbought/oversold interpretation into a view. Do not give
the indicator its own dimension table.

**Date.** 2026-07-25, [[data-warehousing-and-business-intelligence]].

## Why

> "It is tempting to give an indicator its own dimension table, with the value and a pair of
> overbought/oversold flags. That inverts the star"
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/docs/star-schema.md, 2026-07-25

Two arguments, both about what a dimension is *for*. A dimension holds the attributes you slice
**by**; a measure is the thing being sliced. `RSI14` is numeric, continuous, and changes every day —
"nobody slices by a continuous float". See [[measure-vs-dimension]] and
[[relative-strength-index]].

The second argument is the more portable one, and it is about **thresholds**:

> "Storing them freezes one analyst's convention — 70 and 30 — into the warehouse, so moving the
> threshold would mean rewriting history."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/docs/star-schema.md, 2026-07-25

Overbought and oversold are not properties of a trading day. They are a reading applied to a number,
and the number is what the warehouse stores. Materialising the flags would push an analyst's
convention into the persistence layer, where changing it means a rewrite rather than a redefinition.
`dw.vw_QuoteSignals` derives both flags in a view, so the convention is one `CREATE OR ALTER` away
from being different.

## The cost, stated

> "Reached through a dimension keyed by its own surrogate, a day's RSI takes two joins to retrieve a
> value that could simply have been a column."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/docs/star-schema.md, 2026-07-25

[[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]] — the repo states what the rejected design costs rather than
just asserting it is wrong.

## Alternatives rejected

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **`DimRSI` keyed by its own surrogate, carrying value + flags** | inverts the star; a continuous measure becomes something you slice by; two joins to read one number |
| **Materialise `IsOverbought` / `IsOversold` as fact columns** | freezes 70/30 into stored history; a threshold change becomes a backfill |
| **Compute the indicator at query time from close prices** | not named in the repo. **TODO:** whether this was considered is unrecorded — the backfill approach may simply have been the assignment's shape |

## The rejected design is still in the tree

`project/twtr/ssas/Dim RSI.dim` exists, with `RSIKey`, `IsOverbought`, `IsOversold` and `DateKey`
attributes, feeding a second cube (`Twitter_rsi.cube`) whose only measure is a row count. It is
**exactly** the modelling this decision rejects, committed alongside the argument against it. See
[[ssas]] and [[keep-the-superseded-version-in-tree]].

Neither `DimRSI` nor `FactRSI` is created by any committed DDL, so the cube and the schema do not
describe the same database — [[documentation-drift]].

**TODO:** whether the cube was built first and the argument written afterwards, or the artefact kept
deliberately as a worked counter-example, is unrecorded. `confidence: low` on the ordering. The
decision itself is `confidence: high` — argued in the design doc, implemented as a fact column in the
DDL, and carried through by the view and the backfill script, three independent artefacts agreeing.

## Generalisation

The rule this instance teaches is not about indicators. It is: **a derived number is a measure; the
convention used to read it is not data at all.** Anything defined by a cut-off — churn risk bands,
SLA breaches, "large" orders — belongs in a view or a semantic layer, not in stored columns, for
exactly the reason above. See [[star-schema]] and [[fact-grain]].
